summary.text: A triple junction is the point where the boundaries of three tectonic plates meet.
Each of the three boundaries is a ridge, a trench or a transform fault, so junctions are labelled by the mix that meets there, such as R-R-R or F-F-T.
Only a few of the possible types keep their shape through geologic time; the rest change into another form or cannot exist at all.

facts.label: First paper on concept
facts.value: Published in 1969, co-written by Dan McKenzie

facts.label: Failed arm example
facts.value: The Benue Trough, off the Gulf of Guinea

items.prompt: A continent starts to break apart along three spreading arms that radiate from one point. What usually happens next?

options.label: All three arms widen into oceans
One arm fails while two open an ocean
All three arms close up again
The arms turn into deep trenches

items.explain: During continental breakup three divergent boundaries form, but one fails while the other two keep spreading to form an ocean.

items.prompt: Four plates could in theory all meet at a single point. How long would such a meeting point last?
items.explain: A meeting of four or more plates is theoretically possible, but such junctions only exist instantaneously.

items.prompt: Three active faults, each with plates sliding sideways past each other, meet at one point. What becomes of that meeting point?

options.label: It turns into three spreading ridges
It cannot hold a stable shape
It halts all three plates at once

items.explain: Three lines along the sides of a velocity triangle can meet at a point only when there is no relative motion, so an FFF junction with active faults can never be stable.

items.prompt: An unstable meeting of three sideways faults is believed to have created something about 190 million years ago. What?
items.explain: The inherent instability of an FFF junction is believed to have caused the formation of the Pacific plate about 190 million years ago.

items.prompt: Earth is round, yet geologists usually study the motion at a triple junction on a flat diagram. Why does that work?

options.label: Plates are perfectly flat sheets of rock
The area is small, so motion barely varies
Rotation poles always sit at the junction
Gravity flattens the crust near junctions

items.explain: The area around a junction is small compared with Earth and usually far from the rotation pole, so motion along each boundary can be treated as constant on a flat surface.

items.prompt: Three spreading ridges meet at one ideal triple junction. Roughly what angle separates neighbouring ridges?
items.explain: Three divergent boundaries ideally meet at angles near 120°.
